status.text:
Rant time 😈

I implemented and shipped support for MCP at Clerk, I contributed to the MCP spec and SDKs, and I was involved in steering the direction of the protocol in the early days, even attending in-person meetings about it with a variety of industry players.

I am now very strongly against MCP and advise against using it both as a consumer and as a provider. Unfortunately, I don't think there's any going back at this point, but I feel sadly confident that it will waste countless hours of everyone's time over the coming years, when a much easier and better answer is right under our noses.

Let me tell the full story.

thread.text:
Initially, MCP was proposed as a way to allow agents to access users' data from applications that is not public. Things like your emails, your fitness tracker data, etc. This ability was, and still is, an absolute game changer for the overall capabilities of AI agents.

I remember calling a friend of mine for hours, pacing around my neighborhood at 10pm ranting and raving like a lunatic about how big of a deal this was. I made a pitch deck about it and presented it to Clerk's CEO, proposing letting me offload everything else I was working on to go full steam as an IC implementing MCP support for Clerk. Somehow this did end up happening.

It had taken over my mind entirely. I was obsessed.

card.title: How OAuth Works
card.description: A practical guide to OAuth Scoped Access that walks through the Authorization Code Flow with real code examples, security best practices, and clear explanations of how third-party app integrations...

thread.text:
But as I shepherded Clerk's MCP implementation across the line, the disillusionment began. OAuth has been around forever, and is a nearly infinite web of hundreds of different specs, all of which any given consumer or provider may or may not have implemented. There's no ubiquitous way for a provider to know which capacities a consumer wants (though there's an optional spec for that), and same in reverse (also an optional spec for that). There are enterprise grade security features that would probably be valuable for everyone but require alignment between the consumer and provider, so they never really get prioritized (outside of Okta).

Also, the specs change all the time. Especially the MCP spec - if either the consumer or provider side is expecting a different version, too bad. Not to mention that the specs a big and complex and extremely easy to mess up. Even the primary players are constantly messing it up with little bugs and de-syncing from various spec versions, many of which aren't exactly compatible.

While I was working on Clerk's MCP implementation, I found major MCP implementation bugs in both Cursor and Claude Code.

More recently, as a consumer of one of our vendors' MCPs, I noticed I was being signed out every day, they investigated, then came back to tell me that it was not their fault, and was actually a MCP bug in codex (https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/33403).

The second I finished building one OAuth/MCP capability, another one would arrive in the spec that needed to be implemented. New consumers that wanted to use our MCPs were released constantly, many of them not spec compliant, then the user complaints start rolling in, which means you need to run off-spec compatibility workarounds, or just tell the users that they are out of luck until the client they are using fixes some bug.

Dynamic client registration was mandated in the initial version. It's a messy, insecure feature that no provider likes and makes apps much more prone to fraud and abuse. I was in the room when it was decided to try to replace it with something better (now out, CIMD). But DCR will still always need to be supported for compatibility.

It never ends. It never will end.

thread.text:
This begs the question - what do we need all of this code and these specs for, exactly?

The answer: for AI agents to be able to get data from an API.

But wait a minute, do we really need to invent an entire convoluted protocol just for agents to be able to get data from an API?

No, we do not. Agents can easily get data from APIs using API keys. Hand the agent the API key, and it will get the data.

APIs & API keys keys have been around forever. They work great. They require no specs, no protocols, no UI, no URLs. Point the agent at docs or an openapi spec, hand it an API key, and it will get the job done.

Want to limit permissions? A good API key management system includes permission management. This is not a new innovation.

Want to have it expire and force re-auth periodically? You are a sadist, but that is also possible with API keys if you really want.

Want to not allow the agent to directly access the credential? There are many solutions for this - varlock, 1password, etc etc.

Here's the plain truth: you don't need MCP. You can just use API keys.

Honestly, under the hood of every MCP implementation is more than likely an API key system anyway.

thread.text:
So, how did it happen that we got MCP at all?

The initial argument was that agents did not know how to use APIs. They were not smart enough. They would mess it up and fail. They needed dedicated endpoints that they could call into using natural language to get what they needed.

To be fair, this may well have been actually true at the time that MCP was invented. But it’s not true anymore. AI has improved a lot in the last year and a half or so, not like I need to tell anyone that.

Give your agent an API key and it will do just fine. No protocols, no bugs, no re-authentication, it just works.

thread.text:
So here's my call to action:

If you are a company that is trying to make your product accessible to Al agents, build a good API and API key system as your base layer. Then advertise it as the most reliable way to connect an agent!

You will still need to put out an MCP, annoyingly, because your customers will ask for it. But the MCP can just be a cheap wrapper around the API key system, and this is a much more sound architecture. If your users want to torture themselves with MCP, thats their choice. They can always choose to bail once they have had enough, and your API key system will be ready for them.

thread.text:
Bonus rumination: UIs of any sort are losing stock at the fastest rate in software development history.

I don't want your dashboard - I want to ask my agent for the exact information, graph, or action that I need to take, and have it handle that for me.

I don't want your CLI, I'm going to ask my agent to do that, and while sure, it can use your CLI, it can also just hit the API directly. And your CLI is typically a thin wrapper over the API anyway.

Good quality APIs are the absolute most important thing to build out as a company right now. They are the foundation of your product's value. If you want to layer an SDK on top of that, or a CLI, or an MCP later, go for it. You need to meet your customers where they are.

But the API comes first - the rest sit on top. The biggest mistake you can make is to build out one of these higher abstractions first, and have your API be private or only intended to be a proxy for the higher level abstractions. You will end up paying the price for this.

thread.text:
Ok, so I REALLY appreciate all the replies and opinions this post generated. I did not expect this much and I am absolutely floored by the number of people who took the time to read this and leave thoughtful replies, both positive and negative. Feels like a true luxury. I wish I could get this treatment for all my posts!

All the feedback that I have read has meaningfully shaped my opinion here and I want to reflect where I have landed now.

First, MCP carries a lot of value through the simple UX for connecting services. Click button, accept consent, done. I underestimated the weight of this when writing this post. As a developer who is used to dealing with API keys, it feels straightforward for me to go down this path, but that's not the case for everyone.

Especially for products aimed at non-technical users, it's not really an option to ask them to go through an average api key generation and storage flow. I do have ideas on how this could be improved, and will share more about that soon. But it cannot be identical to the two-click MCP flow -- the majority of MCP and OAuth's complexity is in the automated service-to-service credential handoff that enables this flow, and trying to engineer the same UX but with an API key will inevitably lead you right back to OAuth anyway. For developer products and tools however, I stand by my opinion here. Developers know how to use API keys. Save yourself and them the pain and let them just do that.

Second, the enterprise use case is a whole different story. It's no secret that Okta has put a ton of work into both OAuth and MCP, as its a critical component of how enterprise auth works. It makes sense for this use case, and I believe that enterprise auth should continue moving in this direction and entirely ignore my critique.

That being said, enterprise auth is kind of painful. I am sure many of you reading have dealt with it before here or there. When you're a huge company and have thousands of employees, any of whom can be compromised/phished at any time without anyone noticing, and when you are holding on to critical data for enormous numbers of other huge companies, as is the standard for enterprise companies, the way you think about auth and security is very different. Granting access to a subset of hundreds of different tools to a set of employees that changes by the hundreds weekly is a whole different world than hiring someone and manually onboarding them to what they need, like many smaller companies do. This lens creates the need for protocols like saml, scim, directory sync, etc, as well as enterprise access control tools like Okta.

I think what has been bothering me, and what led to this thread, is that I believe that MCP has the security and complexity (and compatibility, and user pain) characteristics of an enterprise auth protocol. Let's not beat around the bush - it is one. However, it's being held up as the standard that everyone should be using, regardless of their audience, even if its a developer tool or a small startup. I believe that there should be a well-known, commonly accepted, simpler integration option available without making every provider and consumer participate in the full OAuth/MCP ecosystem.

For developer products & tools, I think the answer is API keys. There should also be an answer for non-developer products though, and I will be thinking more about how this can be done this week.
